title: Learn to Respond Instead of React
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece draws a sharp line between reacting and responding, framing reaction as impulsive and instinct-driven and response as deliberate and chosen. It argues that leaders are held to a higher standard than most, and that unfiltered reactions -- especially ones tinged with anger or frustration -- damage credibility and escalate conflict. The essay offers a practical mechanism: three screening questions leaders can ask themselves before speaking or acting, aimed at slowing down the impulse to react. It closes by acknowledging the difficulty of this shift for passionate leaders while insisting the discipline pays off.
points: Reaction is impulsive and unconscious; response is deliberate and intentional -- leaders are expected to favor the latter.
Raw, uncensored reactions laced with anger or frustration erode a leader's credibility and escalate negative feelings.
Knowing your personal triggers is a prerequisite for choosing to respond rather than react in the moment.
Before acting, leaders can ask whether they have the facts, have interpreted the situation accurately, and are extending the benefit of the doubt.
The shift from reacting to responding is difficult, especially for candid, passionate leaders, but it is a skill worth building deliberately.
quotes: Reaction is an emotional and reflexive act that is largely unconscious and always impulsive.
In contrast, responding is thoughtful and deliberate. It is a highly intentional and rational decision.
Whenever a leader reacts instinctually, offering raw and uncensored remarks, they become suspect.
Leaders who decide when and how they will respond, as opposed to react, take ownership of the situation and the people involved.
Leaders can never positively influence a negative situation with a bad reaction.
